newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-FURYK AND CLARKE LEAD BRITISH OPEN, 92 FOR BAKER-FINCH.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-FURYK AND CLARKE LEAD BRITISH OPEN, 92 FOR BAKER-FINCH.

text.p: Tiger Woods shot 72 in the British Open on Thursday as wild-swinging American Jim Furyk and powerful Northern Irishman Darren Clarke both tamed Royal Troon's back nine to lead with four-under-par 67s.

The Masters champion's round included a triple-bogey at the 11th hole after he drove into a gorse bush, took a penalty drop, half-fluffed his third, struck an eight iron over the green, chipped and two-putted from six feet.
"My plan was to be patient and I didn't lose it," the 21-year-old world number one said. "Frustrated at the 11th, yes, lose patience, no.
"I maintained it all day and I'm definitely proud of that."
Birdies at the 16th and 18th from 15 and 18 feet hauled the game's new phenomenon back into contention. "They definitely got me into the ball game again," he said.

Furyk and Clarke each played the back nine, which with a fierce headwind more than lived up to its fearsome reputation, in level-par 35 to snatch a two-stroke lead over Australian Greg Norman and Americans Fred Couples and Justin Leonard.

Five players shot 70 including, late in the day, 44-year-old Scottish amateur matchplay champion Barclay Howard, who will play for the Britain and Ireland Walker Cup team against the United States in New York next month.

Five more, including five-times champion Tom Watson and three-times winner Nick Faldo, had level-par 71s as only 16 of the 156-man field matched or bettered par in the testing wind which sent scores soaring on the 7,079-yard links layout.
U.S. Open champion Ernie Els carded a four-over-par 75 while defending champion Tom Lehman shot 74.
The 1991 champion, Ian Baker-Finch of Australia, withdrew after a 21-over-par 92, the highest round at the Open since a 95 by Englishman Guy McQuitty in 1986 at Turnberry.
The Turnberry winner in 1994, Zimbabwean Nick Price, skied to a 78.
Swede Pierre Fulke aced the 179-yard 14th hole with a three-iron, just a week after a achieving a hole-in-one in the first round of the Loch Lomond World Invitational. He ended the day with a 73.
Furyk, 27, has an idiosyncratic swing described as being "like a man trying to kill a snake in a phone booth."
Or "a swing only a mother could love," Furyk added.
Clarke, certain to make Europe's Ryder Cup team this year, birdied four of the first seven holes and also the 11th where he sank a 70-foot putt from the front edge of the green.

Norman, the 1986 and 1993 champion, and Couples, the 1992 Masters champion, made hay on the downwind front nine and then limited the damage coming back into the wind. Norman played the front nine in four-under 32 and the back in two-over 37 while Couples, whose father is seriously ill with leukaemia, shot 31-38 for his 69.
"We are playing two different golf courses out there," said Norman, who dropped shots at the 13th and the last. "The wind is heavy and it is very cold. Coming home you have to hang on.
"You can hit good shots and feel like a fool. I hit 37 shots on the back nine and 15 of them I never ever practice."
Couples has been concerned for the health of his father
after he recently required a course of chemotherapy for his illness.
"I took a month off before the U.S. Open, didn't touch a club and didn't feel like playing," he said. "It wears on you."
Leonard, who won the Kemper Open last month and who has been fifth and third since then, did it the hard way -- two under for the front and then level par 35 on the back.
Later Furyk and Clarke played the back in similar vein after front nines of 32.

But local favourite Colin Montgomerie, the world number four who has missed four of the last five British Open cuts, went to pieces on the course where he played as a boy though he did not blame the wind.
The U.S. Open runner-up could not stop sending his tee shots to the right and hit only the first three fairways in a disappointing five-over-par 76.

American Davis Love, Angel Cabrera of Argentina and Swede Jesper Parnevik, runner-up in 1994, were in the group on 70. Two-times U.S. Open champion Curtis Strange and Ian Woosnam of Britain were on 71.
Watson did not hit any back nine greens in regulation but chipped well to limit the damage to a 38.
"I didn't put myself out of play. That's what you have to do on this golf course," he said.
"Everybody knows what the wind is like. The back nine is one of the toughest nines in golf."
